questions.knowledge_point: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation
questions.problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x{y}^{2}}{x+1}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(\frac{x}{x+1})\cdot {y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x}{x+1}
$$

questions.problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x+y}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{y}
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{e}^{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x},
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
{e}^{-y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡y}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}<y<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡y} \\ {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡y & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡y=x+C.
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}{cos}^{2}⁡y$ for $0<y<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x}{cos}^{2}⁡y \\ \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x} \\ {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡y & ={e}^{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡y={e}^{x}+C.
$$

$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡y={x}^{3}+C.

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{y}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{y}} \\ \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{2{y}^{3/2}}{3} & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+K \\ {y}^{3/2} & ={x}^{3/2}+C \\ \sqrt{{y}^{3}} & =\sqrt{{x}^{3}}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{3K}{2}.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{{x}^{3}}+C.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}$ for $y\ne 0$ and $-\frac{\pi }{2}<x<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=6x\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6x\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\cdot 3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\int {y}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{1/3} & ={x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{1/3}={x}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=({x}^{2}+C)^{3}.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(2x+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}.
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|={x}^{3}+x+C.

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{3}+x+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{3}+x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{3}+x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{{x}^{3}+x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{{x}^{3}+x}.

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}-\sqrt{y}=2x\sqrt{y}$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}-\sqrt{y} & =2x\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\sqrt{y} & =2x\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(2x+1)\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(2x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ 2\sqrt{y} & ={x}^{2}+x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
2\sqrt{y}={x}^{2}+x+C
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}+x+C}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2y}=0$ for $y>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2y} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2y} \\ 2y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2y\,\text{d}y & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{2} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)y=0$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)y \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $x,y \geq 0,$ separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2xy}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  \sqrt{2x} \cdot  \sqrt{y}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{y} \\ y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+2K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C= 2K.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
y^2 = x^2 + C .
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form
canonical_examples.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' = \dfrac {x^2}{y}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}y^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + C.
$$

We can express the solution in the form $y = y(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = 2C.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating
canonical_examples.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' + 2xy = 0$ for $y\neq 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2xy \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln \vert y \vert = -x^2 + C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y = y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = e^C$  and $K > 0.$ 

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y = Ke^{-x^2}.
$$
